clue.text: Out-of-this-world 23 coming together, system rapidly forming

definitions.meaning: the puzzle's theme, sweets sold under astronomical names, and this entry wants two of them side by side

indicators.note: Two things joined into one phrase: the pair of names named by the first half are laid end to end and read as a single answer.

definitions.meaning: astronomers' phrase for a star system making new stars far faster than the usual rate

explanation.surface: Matter out in space clumping together as a new system takes shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 23 down is CANDY, so 'out-of-this-world 23' asks for a sweet with a space name — here two of them, and the pair turns out to be a real term in astronomy.
explanation.definitionFit: Starburst and Galaxy are both sweets named after space, and a starburst galaxy is one turning gas into stars at a furious rate.

clue.text: Say no more, narcissist has doffed cap for supreme Being

indicators.note: Doffing a cap is lifting it off your head, so the word it applies to loses the letter sitting on top of it.

parts.note: the noise you make telling somebody to be quiet, written down as two letters
a diva is somebody entirely wrapped up in herself

explanation.surface: A vain man baring his head, told to stop talking about himself.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital B on 'Being' is the only signal that a god is wanted rather than a person, and 'Say no more' is doing service as two letters instead of the idiom it looks like.
explanation.definitionFit: Shiva is not one god among many but the supreme being of Shaivism, the destroyer and renewer at the head of the Hindu pantheon.

clue.text: Difficult work, or not, opening present

indicators.note: A present being opened has a gap in it, and that gap is where the letters named alongside are dropped.

parts.note: an award is a present in the sense of something formally handed over
WORK told to do without OR keeps only its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Hard work, or maybe not, unwrapping a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Difficult work' reads as one phrase, which is what hides the seam: only the first word is the definition, and the second is about to lose two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Awkward means difficult to handle or deal with — an awkward customer is a difficult one, the same everyday sense.

clue.text: Explicit case of wood in tree

indicators.note: in puts the outer letters inside the tree

parts.note: the bay is a laurel tree

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outer shell, its first and last letters

parts.note: the word wood, whose outside letters are taken

explanation.surface: A carving in a tree's wood turns out to be rather rude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case of' leaves WD from wood, which goes 'in' BAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Bawdy means coarsely humorous about sex, openly explicit in a ribald way.

clue.text: Song about India in raga oddly similar in sound

indicators.note: in places the song-with-letter between the two odd letters
oddly takes the odd-numbered letters, the first and third, of the word

parts.note: the word raga, a form of Indian music

indicators.note: about means going round, so the song wraps the letter

parts.note: a hymn is a religious song
India is I in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A song about India fits oddly inside an Indian raga that sounds alike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts I inside HYMN to make HYMIN; 'oddly' takes R and G from raga, and HYMIN goes 'in' between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyming words share their ending sounds, so they are alike in how they are heard.

clue.text: Child, and corn she has on the backside?

parts.note: a tot is a small child
what she has is hers, and the possessive form of 'she' is these three letters
corn grows in ears, one to a stalk

explanation.surface: A child, and a corn she has on her backside.
explanation.walkthrough: The three pieces straddle the gaps in the answer instead of sitting inside them, so nothing you build lines up with anything you write.
explanation.definitionFit: To the rear means at the back of something, and 'on the backside' puts the same position in blunter, bodily terms.

clue.text: Weed in pig's ear?

definitions.meaning: the smokeable kind, cannabis resin pressed into blocks
to make a pig's ear of a job is British for botching it completely

explanation.surface: Weed growing in a pig's ear.
explanation.walkthrough: Drug slang and kitchen slang sit a preposition apart: the smoker's block of resin, and the mess you make of a job — make a pig's ear of it, make a hash of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hash is cannabis resin, and a hash is also a botch — the same word British idiom pairs with a pig's ear.

clue.text: For 'haunt', try entering an anagram of that!

indicators.note: The setter names the device outright: the letters of the word he has just quoted are to be re-sorted before anything else happens.
Somebody entering a building goes inside it, so the piece named before it is placed within the shuffled letters.

parts.note: 'that' points back at the word in quotation marks, five letters waiting to be shuffled
a go is an attempt at something

explanation.surface: A setter daring you to solve it by rearranging the word he has just handed you.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says exactly what to do and is still hard, because the letters being shuffled are the definition's own — meaning and material come out of the same five letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A hang-out is the place somebody is always to be found, which is precisely what a haunt is, in slangier clothes.

clue.text: Capacity remains for out-of-this-world 23

parts.note: capacity is how much room there is, measured as an amount
what remains of a body in the end, as the funeral service has it

explanation.surface: There is still room for something not of this earth.
explanation.walkthrough: Both wordplay words are nouns pretending to be a verb and its subject — capacity remains. 23 down is CANDY, and the theme is sweets named after space.
explanation.definitionFit: Space Dust is a brand of crackling sherbet, a candy — 23 down — whose name is literally out of this world.

clue.text: Use unknown technique for out-of-this-world 23

parts.note: to milk a situation is to use it for all it is worth
algebra's unknown quantities are X, Y and Z
a way of doing something is the technique you use

explanation.surface: Applying a technique nobody has heard of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Use' is the verb meaning exploit rather than employ. The bar takes its name from the galaxy overhead, which is what earns it a place in this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: A Milky Way is a chocolate bar — a candy, which is 23 down — and it is named for the galaxy we live in.

clue.text: Recovered, trouble far from islander

indicators.note: To recover a thing is to get it back, and 'back' is the instruction — the pieces are read from their far end. A loose signal, and the looseness is the setter's.

parts.note: to nag is to trouble somebody on and on
'far from ready' means not ready, so the phrase stands in for a plain negative

explanation.surface: An islander back on their feet and no trouble to anybody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Far from' hides a whole word — it means 'not', which is half the wordplay. Tonga is a kingdom of some 170 islands in the South Pacific.
explanation.definitionFit: A Tongan is a native of Tonga, an island kingdom in the South Pacific, so 'islander' defines by example.

clue.text: See 1
Divorcee, after breaking up, froze

indicators.note: A marriage breaking up scatters what was joined, and these letters do the same — they will not stay in the order given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters — exactly the enumeration

explanation.surface: A divorcee turning cold on the world once the marriage has ended.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is one sad little story, and that is what stops the first word from looking like eight loose letters waiting to be shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Water that has iced over has frozen at the surface, so 'froze' is the same event in the same tense.

clue.text: Vicious swine sent back in time machine

indicators.note: Something sent back travels the way it came, so in an across entry the assembled pieces are read from right to left.

parts.note: Sid Vicious played bass for the Sex Pistols, and the surname is the half printed here
call somebody a rat and you have called them a swine

explanation.surface: A savage pig posted back through the centuries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vicious' looks like an adjective describing the swine and is really a surname. The Tardis is the police box the Doctor travels in on Doctor Who.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tardis is the blue police box that carries the Doctor through time, so 'time machine' names it by exactly what it does.

clue.text: A river down below capital of Zimbabwe in shade

definitions.note: read as 'in this shade': the answer names a shade of colour

indicators.note: below, in a down entry, means the river comes beneath, so after, the capital letter
the capital, or head, of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the word Zimbabwe, whose first letter is used
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire, England, a crossword favourite
to feel down is to feel blue, sad

explanation.surface: A river runs downhill south of Zimbabwe's capital, its waters a deep colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital of' gives Z, and 'below' sets the river URE beneath it in this down entry; 'down' looks like a direction for the river, but it is a synonym for sad.
explanation.definitionFit: Azure blue is a bright, clear sky-blue colour, a shade of blue.

clue.text: Rags, those sent abroad, insufficient amounts

indicators.note: Things sent abroad are scattered somewhere else entirely, and these letters land in an order of their own.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters, matching the enumeration

explanation.surface: Old clothes shipped overseas, and never enough of them to go round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Those' reads as a pointing word rather than as five more letters, and it is the piece the whole anagram depends on.
explanation.definitionFit: A shortage is a want of something needed, so 'insufficient amounts' spells out the same idea, plural for plural.

clue.text: Dreary lecture, reportedly — that would never take off

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is said out loud, so we want a word that sounds like the phrase

parts.note: dreary means grey and a lecture is a talk, giving grey talk

explanation.surface: A dull lecture is reported as one that would never get off the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Said quickly, 'grey talk' sounds like the bird's name. 'take off' is meant literally: it could not fly.
explanation.definitionFit: The great auk was a large flightless seabird of the North Atlantic, hunted to extinction in the 1840s.

clue.text: Question having caught cold: is spring here?

definitions.note: The definition is put as a question rather than a noun phrase: it asks where you would find a spring, and the answer is the building put up around one.

parts.note: to pump somebody is to press them for information
rheum is the watery stuff a head cold produces, and it is said exactly like the four letters written here

explanation.surface: Somebody streaming with a cold, questioned about whether spring has arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught cold' reads as the idiom for being taken by surprise and is really handing you a doctor's word for the sniffles, to be said aloud. Bath's Pump Room served water from the spring beneath it.
explanation.definitionFit: A pump room is the hall at a spa where water from the spring is pumped up and drunk, so the spring is indeed there.

clue.text: Sweet thing, flower impressed by dancing when excited

indicators.note: impressed by means pressed into, so the jumbled letters are placed inside the flower

parts.note: the poppy is a flower

indicators.note: when excited means once stirred up, so the letters of dancing are jumbled

explanation.surface: A sweetheart, the apple of someone's eye, gets excited dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet thing' sounds like a term of endearment but means a confection, one of the puzzle's space-themed sweets. 'impressed by' sets the jumbled letters inside the flower before its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Popping candy is a fizzing sweet that crackles in the mouth, sold in the UK as Space Dust.

clue.text: Out-of-this-world 23 warps beam

parts.note: to mar a thing is to spoil it, which is what warping does to a shape
a beam is a length of timber or metal laid across a gap

explanation.surface: Something unearthly bending a beam out of true.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warps beam' reads as one action with its object and is two separate synonyms. The bar shares its name with the planet, which is all the theme asks of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A Mars bar is a candy — 23 down — and it carries the name of a planet, which makes it out of this world.

clue.text: Extra tests: restrain oneself, turning tail

indicators.note: the tail, the last two letters, is turned round so its order is reversed

parts.note: to resist is to hold back, to restrain oneself

explanation.surface: Faced with extra exams, a student tries not to run away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning tail' looks like fleeing, but it means flipping the final ST of RESIST.
explanation.definitionFit: Resits are exams taken again after a failure, extra tests for the student.

clue.text: See 24 Across
Old scandalmonger keeping politicians in check

indicators.note: Keeping something means holding on to it inside, so the word beside it closes round the letters named next.

parts.note: to hold somebody in check is to deter them
MPs are Members of Parliament, the elected members of the Commons

explanation.surface: A veteran gossip columnist with the politicians under control.
explanation.walkthrough: Nigel Dempster wrote the Daily Mail's gossip column for a quarter of a century, and 'Old' is the clue's way of saying he is no longer with us.
explanation.definitionFit: Nigel Dempster was Fleet Street's best-known gossip columnist, trading in scandal, and 'Old' marks him as the late one.

clue.text: Eat around a fire

indicators.note: Around means encircling, so the word in front of it wraps itself about the letter that comes next.

parts.note: to lunch is to eat, the verb of the midday meal
the clue's own indefinite article, taken as a single letter

explanation.surface: Eating around a campfire.
explanation.walkthrough: Two ordinary words change job at once: 'fire' is a verb here and 'a' is a letter rather than an article.
explanation.definitionFit: To launch a rocket is to fire it, the sense of setting something off rather than sliding a boat into the water.

clue.text: Chance to win big wasted, lead blown

indicators.note: Blown away is gone for good, so the letter named just before it is missing from the finished word.

parts.note: blotto is British slang for hopelessly drunk
the lead of a word is the letter at its head, and the drunken word above starts with this one

explanation.surface: A jackpot squandered and the lead thrown away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wasted' is the drinker's sense rather than the squanderer's, and 'lead' means a first letter rather than a position in a race.
explanation.definitionFit: Lotto is the numbers draw people play for a jackpot, so 'Chance to win big' describes the game by what it offers.

clue.text: See 17
Out-of-this-world 23, smashing stuff in the kitchen?

definitions.meaning: the sherbet-filled rice-paper discs from the corner shop, named after the UFO
crockery hurled across the room in a domestic row does not stay in one piece

explanation.surface: Something unearthly in a kitchen where the china is already being thrown.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the second half as a joke rather than a dictionary sense: read one word at a time, it describes airborne crockery in a domestic row.
explanation.definitionFit: Flying saucers are sherbet sweets named for the UFO, and saucers genuinely flying are smashing stuff — china in mid-air.

clue.text: Some birds pecked others

parts.note: a bird that pecked you bit you
'others' borrows the birds from the definition and asks for a different sort — the slim sea ones that hover and dive

explanation.surface: A garden scuffle in which one lot of birds goes for the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Others' cannot stand alone: it reaches back into the definition for the word 'birds' and asks for another species, so one word serves two parts of the clue at once.
explanation.definitionFit: Bitterns are the booming brown herons of the reed beds, so 'Some birds' defines by example — a particular few of a large class.

clue.text: Austrian maestro with an uber-Germanic piece

indicators.note: A piece of something is a fragment broken off it, so what is wanted is an unbroken run of letters out of the words beside it.

parts.note: four letters in a row here, straddling the hyphen

explanation.surface: An Austrian conductor playing a very German piece of music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece' reads as a piece of music, which is exactly where the surface wants your mind. Alban Berg wrote Wozzeck and studied under Schoenberg in Vienna.
explanation.definitionFit: Alban Berg was the Viennese composer of Wozzeck and Lulu, so 'Austrian maestro' names him by nationality and trade.

clue.text: Very much for the love of God!

definitions.meaning: as in doubting a thing very much — the adverb meaning to a great degree
the exasperated cry of somebody whose patience has just run out

explanation.surface: Something done wholeheartedly out of love for God.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as piety and means impatience: 'for the love of God!' is what people say at the end of their tether, and the answer is the one-word version of it.
explanation.definitionFit: One word covers both: the adverb meaning to a great degree, and the single-word groan of exasperation thrown at somebody trying your patience.
